title: CreateView, UpdateView, DeleteView
description: Handle creation, editing, and deletion of objects with minimal code.

slides.title: CRUD in One Go ✍️
slides.content:
Django provides generic views for create, update, and delete operations. They combine form handling and redirects.

- `CreateView` – displays a form to create a new object, saves on POST.
- `UpdateView` – displays a form pre‑filled with an existing object, updates on POST.
- `DeleteView` – asks for confirmation, then deletes the object.

slides.title: CreateView Example
slides.content:
from django.views.generic import CreateView
from django.urls import reverse_lazy
from .models import Post
from .forms import PostForm

class PostCreateView(CreateView):
    model = Post
    form_class = PostForm          # optional; if not set, uses a ModelForm
    template_name = 'posts/create.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post_list')  # where to redirect after success

quizData.question: What is the purpose of `reverse_lazy` in a generic view?

options.text: To avoid URL reversal errors when the URLconf hasn't loaded yet
To automatically set the success URL

quizData.explanation: `reverse_lazy` delays URL reversal until the view is called, avoiding import issues when the URLconf is not fully loaded.

slides.title: UpdateView and DeleteView
slides.content:
from django.views.generic import UpdateView, DeleteView

class PostUpdateView(UpdateView):
    model = Post
    fields = ['title', 'content']  # which fields to edit
    template_name = 'posts/update.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post_list')

class PostDeleteView(DeleteView):
    model = Post
    template_name = 'posts/delete_confirm.html'
    success_url = reverse_lazy('post_list')

# DeleteView automatically asks for confirmation via a template (default: app/model_confirm_delete.html)

slides.title: Customizing the Redirect
Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
## Set `success_url` to a named URL

Using `reverse_lazy` ensures you don't get import errors. Always use `reverse_lazy` in class attributes.
